notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, as reported to the MA Division of Local Services on Schedule A, not a budget.

Includes public schools. Massachusetts cities and towns pay for their schools and their share of any regional school district through the town budget, where most other states have separate school districts, so spending and property tax per resident run higher than in those states.

Covers the general fund, special revenue funds (federal and state grants, school lunch, revolving and other special revenue), capital projects and enterprise funds such as water and sewer: $836,314,538 of revenue and $1,266,155,383 of spending outside the general fund. Trust funds, transfers between funds and borrowing are left out. Capital projects spent $458,088,790 more than they took in, which is generally paid with bonds. Fire, water and other districts inside the town are separate governments and are not included.
Debt is all long-term debt the town reported outstanding at the end of FY 2025 (Schedule A Part 10), including school construction and any water, sewer or other enterprise fund borrowing.
"Taxes" on Schedule A include motor vehicle and other local excises ($324,511,629), which are shown as other local taxes. The rest, with penalties and interest, is shown as property tax.

Fixed costs ($927,382,178: health insurance, pensions and other benefits for town and school staff) are spread across departments in proportion to their size, schools included, as with benefits in other states. Debt service is left out of that spread.
Intergovernmental assessments and other spending ($378,127,008: charter school tuition, regional transit and county and state charges) are spread across departments in proportion to their size.

Political money counts contributions from unions and registered PACs to Boston's party ward, town and city committees and its candidates for mayor and city council, filed with the Office of Campaign and Political Finance since 2023. Corporate contributions are banned in Massachusetts. Individuals and money passed between candidate and party committees are not counted. Candidates for other offices file with the city clerk, so their own committees are not included, and party committees also support state candidates.

Transparency: City of Boston has filed its Schedule A annual financial report with the Division of Local Services for FY 2025, the latest year most MA governments have filed. This is a check that the report was filed, not an opinion on its contents. The other five practices have not been checked yet, so they are left out of the score.

Cameras: 46 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Boston's borders in OpenStreetMap (25 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Massachusetts yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Flock camera network
redFlags.detail: 25 Flock Safety license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Boston's borders in OpenStreetMap. Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is recorded for some; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.

source.label: OpenStreetMap license-plate cameras (as mapped by DeFlock)

redFlags.label: Third-party investigative platform
redFlags.detail: The Boston Police Department has access to SoundThinking's CrimeTracer (formerly Coplink X) investigative platform through a statewide contract announced in December 2022.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS013104, citing ShotSpotter

redFlags.unscoredReason: Not scored: every police department in the state has this through a statewide contract, so it is not a local decision.

redFlags.label: Third-party investigative platform
redFlags.detail: The Boston Regional Intelligence Center uses LexisNexis' Accurint investigative platform.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS014778, citing ACLU

redFlags.label: Police drones
redFlags.detail: The Boston Police Department operates three drones as of 2017, according to data compiled by the Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS003061, citing Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College

redFlags.label: Cell-site simulator
redFlags.detail: The Boston Police Department uses a cell-site simulator, as of 2024.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS004047, citing City of Boston

redFlags.label: Gunshot detection (ShotSpotter)
redFlags.detail: The Boston Police Department used ShotSpotter gunshot detection technology, as of 2024.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS006755, citing City of Boston

redFlags.label: License-plate readers
redFlags.detail: The Boston Police Department used automated license plate readers as of 2024.

notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, as reported to the MA Division of Local Services on Schedule A, not a budget.

Includes public schools. Massachusetts cities and towns pay for their schools and their share of any regional school district through the town budget, where most other states have separate school districts, so spending and property tax per resident run higher than in those states.

Covers the general fund, special revenue funds (federal and state grants, school lunch, revolving and other special revenue), capital projects and enterprise funds such as water and sewer: $83,993,721 of revenue and $133,625,591 of spending outside the general fund. Trust funds, transfers between funds and borrowing are left out. Capital projects spent $41,409,761 more than they took in, which is generally paid with bonds. Fire, water and other districts inside the town are separate governments and are not included.
Debt is all long-term debt the town reported outstanding at the end of FY 2025 (Schedule A Part 10), including school construction and any water, sewer or other enterprise fund borrowing.
"Taxes" on Schedule A include motor vehicle and other local excises ($11,880,558), which are shown as other local taxes. The rest, with penalties and interest, is shown as property tax.
Left out: transfers in from the town's own funds ($4,566,971) and other financing sources such as bond proceeds ($0), which are not new revenue.

Fixed costs ($80,678,101: health insurance, pensions and other benefits for town and school staff) are spread across departments in proportion to their size, schools included, as with benefits in other states. Debt service is left out of that spread.
Intergovernmental assessments and other spending ($22,841,030: charter school tuition, regional transit and county and state charges) are spread across departments in proportion to their size.

Political money counts contributions from unions and registered PACs to Revere's party ward, town and city committees and its candidates for mayor and city council, filed with the Office of Campaign and Political Finance since 2023. Corporate contributions are banned in Massachusetts. Individuals and money passed between candidate and party committees are not counted. Candidates for other offices file with the city clerk, so their own committees are not included, and party committees also support state candidates.

Transparency: City of Revere has filed its Schedule A annual financial report with the Division of Local Services for FY 2025, the latest year most MA governments have filed. This is a check that the report was filed, not an opinion on its contents. The other five practices have not been checked yet, so they are left out of the score.

Cameras: 18 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Revere's borders in OpenStreetMap (18 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Massachusetts yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.detail: 18 Flock Safety license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Revere's borders in OpenStreetMap. Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is recorded for some; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.
